mcqs.question: Which of the following best describes a solenoid?

options.A: A straight piece of wire with no turns
options.B: A coil of wire wound in a helix shape
options.C: A pair of permanent magnets placed side by side
options.D: A battery connected to a lamp

mcqs.answer: A coil of wire wound in a helix shape
mcqs.explanation: A solenoid is a length of insulated wire wound tightly in a helical (coil) form. When electric current passes through the coil, it produces a magnetic field similar to that of a bar magnet. Option B correctly defines a solenoid, while the other options describe unrelated objects.

mcqs.learning_point: Understand magnetic field of a solenoid
mcqs.question: When the current in a long solenoid appears clockwise when viewed from one end, the magnetic field inside the solenoid is directed:

options.A: From north to south outside the solenoid
options.B: From south to north outside the solenoid
options.C: From south to north inside the solenoid
options.D: There is no magnetic field inside the solenoid

mcqs.answer: From south to north inside the solenoid
mcqs.explanation: Using the right‑hand rule, curl the fingers of the right hand in the direction of the current (clockwise as seen). The thumb points in the direction of the magnetic field inside the coil, which is from the south pole toward the north pole, i.e., from south to north. Hence option C is correct. Options A and B describe the external field direction, and D is false because a current‑carrying solenoid always produces an internal field.

mcqs.question: How does an electromagnet differ from a permanent magnet?

options.A: It does not produce any magnetic field at all
options.B: Its magnetic field can be switched on or off by controlling the electric current
options.C: It is always stronger than any permanent magnet
options.D: It is made of wood instead of metal

mcqs.answer: Its magnetic field can be switched on or off by controlling the electric current
mcqs.explanation: An electromagnet consists of a coil of wire (often wound around an iron core) through which electric current flows. The magnetic field exists only while current flows, so it can be turned on or off. This distinguishes it from a permanent magnet, whose field is always present. Options A, C, and D are incorrect statements.

mcqs.question: Which of the following changes will increase the strength of an electromagnet?

options.A: Decreasing the number of turns in the coil
options.B: Using a thinner wire for the coil
options.C: Increasing the current flowing through the coil
options.D: Removing the iron core from the coil

mcqs.answer: Increasing the current flowing through the coil
mcqs.explanation: The magnetic field (B) of an electromagnet is proportional to the product of the number of turns (N) and the current (I): B ∝ N·I. Raising the current directly increases the field strength, making option C correct. Reducing turns, using a thinner wire (which raises resistance and may reduce current), or removing the iron core (which concentrates the field) would all weaken the electromagnet.

mcqs.question: Which of the following devices uses an electromagnet to operate?
mcqs.explanation: An electric bell contains a coil that becomes magnetized when current passes through it, attracting a ferromagnetic armature to produce the ringing sound. This is a classic application of an electromagnet. The other items listed have no electromagnetic components.

mcqs.question: A student wraps a long insulated copper wire around a cylindrical tube to make a device that can pick up small metal objects when connected to a battery. Which description best matches this device?
mcqs.explanation: The described device is a coil of wire (solenoid) that, when current flows, creates a magnetic field capable of attracting ferromagnetic objects. Capacitors store charge, resistors limit current, and diodes allow current in one direction; none fit the scenario.

mcqs.learning_point: Understand magnetic field of a solenoid
mcqs.question: A common misconception is that the magnetic field inside a solenoid is weaker than the field outside it. Which statement correctly refutes this misconception?

options.A: The field inside a long solenoid is uniform and much stronger than the external field.
options.B: The field inside a solenoid is zero because the wires cancel each other's effect.
options.C: The external field is always stronger than the internal field.
options.D: A solenoid does not produce any magnetic field at all.

mcqs.answer: The field inside a long solenoid is uniform and much stronger than the external field.
mcqs.explanation: Inside a long solenoid the magnetic field lines are parallel, closely spaced, and nearly uniform, giving a strong field. Outside, the field lines spread out and are much weaker. Hence option A correctly addresses the misconception. Options B, C, and D are false statements.

mcqs.question: If the current through an electromagnet is doubled while the number of turns and the core material remain unchanged, what happens to the magnetic field strength?
mcqs.explanation: Magnetic field strength (B) of an electromagnet is directly proportional to the current (I) flowing through the coil (B ∝ N·I). Doubling I while keeping N constant doubles B. Therefore option C is correct; the other options misrepresent the linear relationship.
